title: ‘Flying blind’: Why experts fear Treasury’s China biotech investment crackdown will backfire
Genomic Reassurance and Diagnostic Closure in Precision Oncology: A Preventable Hazard.
desc: [Clinical pharmacology and therapeutics] Genomic findings can sharpen therapeutic decisions, but they can also provide false reassurance. In precision oncology, labels such as benign, nonactionable, or explanatory may be mistaken for evidence that symptoms or abnormal findings require no further evaluation. This Perspective argues that genotype-phenotype discordance should be treated as a safety signal. Simple report language, tumor-board checks, and artificial intelligence guardrails can preserve the value of genomics without allowing a molecular explanation to become diagnostic closure.

title: Answer or Defer? Testing VLMs' Stated Confidence on Brain MRI
desc: Vision-language models (VLMs) could support medical-image interpretation, but their use requires deciding which interpretations to accept and which images to refer to a clinician. We test whether thresholding stated confidence can retain useful coverage while limiting errors among accepted answers, and how this depends on the population. Eight open-weight VLMs, including two reasoning models, assess 3,888 brain MRI slices from post-treatment glioma patients (BraTS 2024) and healthy volunteers (IXI) for tumor or gross abnormality. BraTS labels are mask-derived; IXI slices are treated as negatives. On BraTS, no threshold selects a nonempty set with at most 5% empirical error for any model, even when chosen retrospectively. This also holds for four models evaluated on a large-lesion, distant-negative subset. At a 10% error budget, Gemma-4-12B retains 24.4% of slices and every other model at most 2.5%. To investigate this limited selection ability, we separate confidence differences between predicted answers from differences within each answer. For four models with available outcome-level summaries, pooled mean confidence differs more between answers than between correct and incorrect responses within each answer. A covariance decomposition explains how this pattern can produce opposite confidence-correctness associations across populations. At a 20% error budget, accepting every "tumor" answer covers more slices than any confidence threshold for two models. These findings caution against using unvalidated stated confidence as a standalone deferral signal and support population-specific validation before deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/amir-sbg/VLM-Answer-or-Defer.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Supervision and Training of Psychologists and Other Mental Health Professionals: A Scoping Review.
desc: [Clinical psychology & psychotherapy] Clinical supervision is fundamental to the development of competent mental health professionals; however, established approaches are limited by challenges in scalability, direct observation and timely feedback. Artificial intelligence has emerged as a potential adjunct to supervision and clinical training, yet the full scope of existing applications has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review systematically mapped artificial intelligence applications in the clinical supervision and training of psychologists and other mental health professionals. The review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported following the PRISMA-ScR. The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. Searches were conducted in nine databases, with supplementary searches in Google Scholar. Two reviewers independently screened records; charted data were checked against the original reports. Database searches identified 11,975 records; 4381 duplicates were removed, 7594 records were screened, 817 reports were assessed for eligibility and 73 sources of evidence were included. Four application categories were identified: virtual patient simulation, automated performance assessment, artificial intelligence-enhanced supervisory feedback and training analytics. Most studies were published from 2022 onward and were concentrated in structured therapies, university-based settings and high-income countries. Artificial intelligence is best positioned as an adjunct that expands opportunities for practice, observation and structured feedback, rather than as a replacement for human supervision. Future research should employ more rigorous designs, validated competency measures, transparent reporting of artificial intelligence systems and outcomes relevant to trainees, supervisors and clients.

title: The Average Patient: Do Simulated Psychiatric Patients Answer Like Real People?
desc: Language models are used as simulated psychiatric patients to train clinicians and evaluate AI therapists, and are judged by plausibility or total scores. We give a framework for simulated respondents: an information budget bounds how much simulated patients can differ, and an average-patient hypothesis, that a model answers each item at the level typical of the named condition and severity, implies little variation, a full profile of the condition's typical symptoms and totals at or above the top of the stated severity band. We examine these implications at matched totals on item-level data from eight human samples, including a clinical and an instructed-feigning sample. Across 17 models, simulated patients vary 1.5 to 11 times less than real respondents with the same total and on most questionnaires endorse nearly every symptom at a middling level; on the PHQ-9 their symptoms covary less like real ones. People, honest or feigning, answer "not at all" about as often as genuine patients with the same totals, and more often than every model. Single answers are highly concentrated, and prompt changes, published personas, larger models and reasoning reduce the pattern without removing it. In interviews, patients told a severity are rated as having nearly every symptom, so an assessment agent's recognition of absent symptoms goes untested, and scored against the stated severity the agent places a quarter of them in their band, against about half of patients given a real symptom profile. Having the model word such a profile restores half to two thirds of the variation.

title: Is More Perceived Empathy Better? Large Language Models, Communication, and Safety in Health Care.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Richter and colleagues offer a careful systematic review of how large language model-based tools affect physician-patient communication, but the outcomes that matter most in deciding to scale a solution-trust and safety-are still unknown. Before deploying these tools, health systems need local validation, ongoing monitoring for accuracy and equity, and pragmatic trials that measure trust, safety, and outcomes alongside perceived empathy.

title: Evidence-Grounded Iterative Reasoning for the Diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases
desc: Overlapping imaging manifestations complicate the differential diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases (DCLDs), while limited annotated data constrain supervised model development. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can integrate imaging and clinical information, but their diagnostic reasoning remains limited by incomplete volumetric perception and insufficient grounding in disease-specific evidence. We propose DCLDs-EIR, an evidence-grounded iterative reasoning framework coupling diagnostic hypothesis refinement with multimodal evidence acquisition and verification. Multiview renderings of predicted lung and cyst segmentations characterize global cyst distributions and initialize the differential diagnosis. Competing hypotheses guide axial CT inspection to identify local findings that, together with clinical context, inform retrieval from a disease-specific knowledge graph. Accumulated patient observations and retrieved knowledge are jointly assessed for diagnostic support and refutation to revise the diagnostic state. Updated hypotheses and unresolved distinctions guide subsequent inspection, forming a feedback loop between evidence acquisition and hypothesis verification. Multicenter evaluation demonstrates that DCLDs-EIR consistently improves diagnostic accuracy over baselines and enables traceable differential diagnosis through explicit links between diagnostic hypotheses, patient observations, and disease-specific knowledge.

title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.
desc: [Frontiers in surgery] This review examines the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the perioperative management of emergency trauma. Published studies suggest performance advantages of AI over traditional methods in prehospital triage, radiographic injury detection, massive transfusion prediction, and early warning of postoperative complications, although findings vary across study designs and validation settings. However, actual adoption in trauma care remains limited due to data heterogeneity, performance degradation in external validation, workflow integration challenges, lack of interpretability, and a scarcity of prospective interventional evidence. This review further argues that methodologically inflated benchmark performance constitutes an underrecognized barrier to adoption in its own right, and that bridging the implementation gap will likely require a shift from area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)-centered reporting toward reporting sensitivity at prespecified clinical thresholds and evaluating patient outcomes in prospective interventional trials.

title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
desc: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.

title: Synergizing New Approach Methodologies and Artificial Intelligence: Charting the Paradigm Shift Toward Next-Generation Chemical Risk Assessment.
desc: [Environmental pollution (Barking, Essex : 1987)] The escalating global chemical inventory, coupled with the ethical and scientific inadequacies of traditional animal testing, has made a change in approach unavoidable in chemical risk assessment. This review examines how the combined use of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping this field. NAMs-including micro physiological systems, high-content screening, multi-omics, and in silico tools-generate high-dimensional and mechanism-anchored data. Concurrently, AI, spanning advanced machine learning and generative models, serves as the essential integrative engine that converts this data into actionable toxicological insight. We present a framework delineating how these two streams of technology interact to operationalize Next-Generation Risk Assessment (NGRA) across its entire pipeline-from intelligent hazard identification and refined exposure prediction to dynamic, population-aware risk characterization. The evidence indicates a shift from empirical, observation-based toxicology toward a predictive, mechanism-centric, and personalized science. By mapping specific AI techniques to core NAMs data streams and NGRA decision points across the hazard, exposure, and risk characterization continuum, this review provides a coherent roadmap for regulators, researchers, and industry stakeholders. We also consider environmental applications, including complex mixtures, persistent organic pollutants (POPs), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), and emerging contaminants, while noting that the supporting evidence is more limited than for human health endpoints. Finally, we critically examine remaining challenges and chart forward-looking paths, including the development of chemical "digital twins," causal AI models, and real-time risk warning systems. We argue that progress depends on integrating NAMs and AI within a more efficient, ethical, and protective global chemical safety framework. However, barriers remain, including limited reproducibility across chemical domains, inadequate external validation, the hallucination risk of large language models in regulatory contexts, and the gap between academic development and regulatory acceptance. Open data infrastructure, standardized benchmarking, and harmonized validation frameworks will be essential to realize the full potential of this approach.

title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography
desc: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.

title: Leveraging Deep Learning to Reveal Fine-Scale In Vivo Mitochondrial Dynamics and Axonal Transport.
source: PubMed · The Yale journal of biology and medicine
desc: [The Yale journal of biology and medicine] In axons, mitochondrial transport is essential for neuronal function and survival, and its disruption is increasingly recognized as an early pathological hallmark in multiple neurodegenerative diseases. Despite its importance, quantitative analysis of mitochondrial transport dynamics remains challenging due to complex and heterogeneous motility patterns and reliance on labor-intensive manual tracking methods. Here, we present a deep learning-assisted framework for semiautomated quantification of mitochondrial axonal transport. Using time-lapse confocal imaging of individual in vivo axons in the well-established Drosophila nervous system, we comprehensively validated transport parameters, including displacement and velocity. We further assessed the fidelity of our method in recapitulating expert-derived measurements and its potential to overcome the limitations of conventional manual tracking. Notably, our framework enables detailed characterization of dynamic behaviors during transport, including intensity-based variations and concurrent morphological changes within individual mitochondria, potentially reflecting mitochondrial physiological states that were difficult to resolve with traditional approaches. Collectively, our study establishes the feasibility of next-generation analysis for axonal transport and highlights its potential to uncover previously inaccessible aspects of mitochondrial dynamics, providing a scalable and objective framework for investigating mitochondrial in vivo transport dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease models.

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
desc: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

title: EZpred: Improving Deep Learning-Based Enzyme Function Prediction Using Unlabeled Sequence Homologs.
desc: [Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)] Features extracted from sequence homologs significantly enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based protein structure prediction. Indeed, homolog-aware models such as AlphaFold generally produce more accurate protein structures compared to single sequence-based methods like ESMfold. In contrast, features from sequence homologs are seldom employed for deep learning-based prediction of the biological functions of a protein, such as Gene Ontology terms or Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers. Although a small number of models also incorporate function labels from sequence homologs, they cannot utilize features extracted from homologs that lack function labels. To address this gap, we developed EZpred, which is the first deep learning model to use sequence homologs by extracting their sequence features while ignoring any function labels. Starting with the target sequence and homologs identified by MMseqs2, EZpred extracts sequence features using the ESM-C protein language model. These features are then fed into a deep learning model to predict the EC numbers of the target protein. For test enzymes with < 30% sequence identity to any training proteins, the F1-score of EZpred EC number prediction is at least 34% higher than state-of-the-art EC number prediction models. These results demonstrate the strong positive impact of sequence homologs in deep learning-based enzyme function prediction.

title: PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations
desc: Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

title: From Precision to Intelligence: The Evolution of Intraoral Scanning.
source: PubMed · Compendium of continuing education in dentistry (Jamesburg, N.J. : 1995)
desc: [Compendium of continuing education in dentistry (Jamesburg, N.J. : 1995)] Intraoral scanning has evolved from a promising alternative to conventional impressions to a mainstream data-acquisition tool across nearly every dental field. As adoption has matured, however, the clinically relevant issue has shifted: it is no longer whether intraoral scanners (IOSs) are accurate enough, but rather under which conditions their accuracy holds and how artificial intelligence (AI) is now being integrated into the scanning process itself to close the remaining gaps. This article revisits the evidence on IOS accuracy and assesses the emerging role of AI-driven software and supporting hardware in improving scan reliability, particularly in demanding clinical scenarios such as complete arch and implants.

title: Odds-Structured Distributional Regression for Interpretable Time-to-Event Prediction
desc: Time-to-event prediction is fundamentally challenged by partial observability and aleatoric uncertainty. In clinical medicine, for instance, the timing of disease progression or acute readmission is contingent on highly dynamic and largely latent health trajectories. Rather than forcing a deterministic point forecast, distributional regression offers a principled means to address this complexity by predicting a probability distribution over time. However, explaining these distributional predictions presents a key obstacle: raw distribution parameters output by the model are abstract mathematical quantities that do not align well with domain concepts. To gain interpretability, we propose a novel paradigm where output parameters are designed to be additive in log-odds---a widely established measure in clinical risk modeling. Our approach, called ODDS-DR, moves beyond technical convenience to deliver clear domain alignment as well as the layer-wise computational structure required for robust, time-dependent feature attribution. Validated across two real-world clinical cohorts, our framework matches state-of-the-art predictive performance while resolving distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Urine Volatomic Assay for Multi-Cancer Detection: A Multicentric Case-Control Discovery and Internal Validation Study.
desc: [Cancer reports (Hoboken, N.J.)] Multi-cancer detection assays may extend early-detection efforts beyond organ-specific screening programs and support emerging models of oncologic primary care, including age- and risk-stratified multi-cancer screening. We evaluated urine volatile organic compound profiles (volatome), an emerging biomarker source, for its association with cancer detection. To determine whether urinary volatome profiles measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and interpreted with artificial intelligence (AI) distinguish participants with known cancer from cancer-free controls and support exploratory tissue-of-origin (TOO) and stage classification. This multicenter retrospective case-control discovery study included urine from 491 treatment-naive participants with one of 10 cancers each and 200 cancer-free healthy controls. Three participating sites contributed de-identified specimens. Volatome profiles were measured by GC-MS. A proprietary ensemble tree-based AI pipeline underwent repeated stratified fivefold internal cross-validation. Preprocessing was fitted within each training partition. Each participant contributed one sample and was assigned only once within a given fold partition. The reported cancer-signal operating point targeted 98% specificity. TOO analysis identified the most likely cancer type and its presumed tissue of origin. The cancer-signal classifier produced an out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.990 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.984-0.996). At the reported 98% specificity-optimized cutoff, sensitivity was 91.9% (451/491). The positive predictive value (PPV) was 99.1% with the cohort's 71% (491/691) cancer prevalence. Grouped TOO accuracy was 91.6% (450/491; 95% CI, 89.2%-94.1%). Among 374 cancers with a recorded stage, the early-versus-late detection classifier had an AUC of 0.866, and it correctly assigned 98.1% (252/257) of early-stage cancers to the early class while recovering 25.6% (30/117) of the late-stage cancers. Recursive removal with high feature importance values produced a small, gradual decline rather than an abrupt loss of performance across the evaluated classification tasks. Urinary VOC profiles contained a composite signal that discriminated known cancer cases from cancer-free controls under internal cross-validation with signals that were able to identify TOO with reasonable certainty.
